title: What are the Benefits of a One Time Mandate in SIP?
summary: What a one-time mandate in a SIP is, how its limit differs from your instalment, when debits happen and what a failed SIP debit means.
body_markdown:
## What is a one-time mandate in a SIP?


A one-time mandate (OTM) is an instruction you give your bank once. It lets the bank pay your fund house (the company that runs the fund) up to a set limit each time you invest. That is how SIP instalments leave your account without you doing anything each month.


A SIP (systematic investment plan) means investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually monthly. Our guide to the[systematic investment plan](https://koshex.com/blog/systematic-investment-plan-sip) covers how that works.


One fund house's scheme document (the official document a fund house publishes for each fund, setting out its terms) puts it this way. You submit a mandate registration form. That authorises your bank to debit your account up to a specified limit per transaction, whenever the fund house asks. You do not send a cheque or a fund transfer letter each time after that. The instruction is to your bank, not to the fund house.


Scheme documents let you pay a SIP through NACH, the national system for recurring bank debits. Another fund house's scheme document says NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India) launched it, and that each NACH mandate gets a unique mandate reference number, called a UMRN. Think of it as the mandate's own ID.


Fund houses accept other routes too. Scheme documents name direct debit at specified banks, where the fund house collects straight from your account, and a standing instruction. With a standing instruction, your bank itself sends the payment. One fund house says SIPs paid by post-dated cheques will not be accepted.


Your SIP money goes from your bank account straight to the fund. A distributor such as Koshex never holds it, and the bank mandate is not in our name. A distributor is a registered intermediary that helps you buy and manage funds.


## How is the mandate limit different from your SIP amount?


The limit is the most your bank will pay on any one debit, while each debit is only the instalment actually due.


Several SIPs, and later one-off purchases, can run under the same mandate as long as each debit fits under it.


Say you run a ₹4,000 SIP and a ₹3,000 SIP under one mandate with a ₹10,000 limit. Each debit, ₹4,000 or ₹3,000, fits. A ₹12,000 extra purchase paid under that mandate later would not.


Step-ups, where your SIP instalment rises by a fixed amount or percentage at set intervals, need the same care. One scheme document says the most a stepped-up instalment may reach must be lower than or equal to the maximum amount in the bank mandate. If the two differ, the lower one is used. A stepped-up instalment cannot go above the mandate's ceiling in that scheme. So set the limit high enough for the largest instalment you expect, including step-ups. The[step-up SIP guide](https://koshex.com/blog/step-up-sip) has the step-up terms.


The number on the mandate is the figure you choose. Ask your bank whether it sets a ceiling of its own. How much to invest each month is a separate question, and[this guide](https://koshex.com/blog/how-much-should-i-invest-in-mutual-funds-every-month) works through it.


A separate rule applies to card and UPI mandates. RBI, India's central bank, lets mutual fund payments of up to ₹1,00,000 a transaction go through without an extra identity check. That is not a cap on your SIP. It only says when the extra check can be skipped.


## How do you set up a mandate?


You fill in the fund house's or platform's mandate form, or approve an e-mandate, and your bank registers it. An e-mandate is one you approve online, by card or UPI.


Timing matters here, and it comes from one fund house's scheme document. If the mandate form and the SIP form go in together, debits may start only after your bank registers the mandate. Once a one-time mandate is registered, a new SIP under it takes up to five business days to set up. That fund house also asks for the SIP request at least 21 business days before the first debit.


For card and UPI mandates, RBI's rules say the e-mandate is registered only after an extra identity check, and the first transaction needs one too. For UPI AutoPay, the recurring-payment feature in UPI apps, NPCI's rules say any action you take on a mandate needs your UPI PIN.


Banks may charge for setting up a mandate. SBI's schedule of charges, updated 30 September 2025, lists ₹50 plus GST for "One time Mandate Authorisation". Other banks set their own charges, so check your bank's schedule.


To see the whole process of buying a fund, read[how to invest in mutual funds online or offline](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-invest-in-mutual-funds-online-offline-in-india) .


## When is your SIP amount debited, and why might it not be?


One scheme document says the debit happens on the SIP date you chose, or the next business day if that date is a holiday.


The same document allows any date from the 1st to the 28th for monthly SIPs.


Your units are priced at the NAV (the price of one unit) of the day the money reaches the fund and is available to it. For most funds, money must reach the scheme's account by 3:00 pm for that day's NAV. Liquid and overnight funds follow different timings. Our note on[cut-off timings](https://koshex.com/blog/mutual-fund-cut-off-timings-all-you-need-to-know) has the detail.


You get a confirmation by email or SMS within five working days. A consolidated account statement follows by the 15th of the next month. It is a statement of your mutual fund transactions, sent for every month in which you had one.


For card and UPI mandates, your bank or card issuer must notify you at least 24 hours before each debit.


Here are some reasons a debit may not go through:


- Your account does not have enough balance on the day.
- Your bank has not yet registered the mandate.
- The instalment is above the mandate's limit.
- The SIP request came too late for the first date you picked.


Timing your date helps with the first one. Say your salary lands on the 1st and your SIP is set for the 5th. The money is already in your account by then. Pick a date after your income arrives, so the balance is there when the debit comes.


## What happens if a SIP debit fails?


That month's instalment buys no units, and everything you have already invested stays invested.


The SIP itself carries on, unless it reaches the failure count below. After the first failed debit, the fund house or its registrar must write to you, saying the SIP will cease if the debits keep failing. A registrar is the firm that keeps investor records and handles transactions for fund houses.


SEBI, the market regulator, has a rule that binds every fund house. A daily, weekly, fortnightly or monthly SIP is treated as cancelled after three failed debit attempts. A bi-monthly, quarterly or longer SIP is cancelled after two. The fund house must also tell you once it cancels.


CAMS, one such registrar, reads the count as consecutive failures. A successful instalment resets it. It also says a pause is not counted as a failed transaction.


Your bank may charge for the failed debit. For example, SBI's schedule of charges (updated 30 September 2025) lists ₹250 plus GST for a failed mandate. Charges differ from bank to bank.


### Can you make up a missed month?


Only with a separate extra purchase in the same fund, which buys units at that day's NAV. One scheme document sets the minimum for such an additional purchase at ₹100. The SIP does not count it as the missed instalment. The failed instalment stays failed for the cancellation count.


A SIP is not a loan, so a missed instalment is not a missed loan repayment.


### What if you plan to skip a month or two?


A pause, where your fund house offers one, is meant for this. One fund house allows a pause of 1 to 6 months, after which the SIP restarts by itself. Its pause does not work for SIPs paid by a bank standing instruction. See[how to stop or pause a SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-stop-or-pause-a-sip) for the detail. Koshex customers can pause a SIP on Koshex.


If the reason is a market fall, read[should you redeem your funds when markets are down](https://koshex.com/blog/should-i-redeem-my-funds-since-the-markets-are-down) first. Koshex also talks you through sharp falls before you redeem.


## Can you change or cancel a mandate?


You can cancel a SIP at any time, and card or UPI e-mandates can be withdrawn at any time. Either stops the future debits it covers.


For the SIP: every platform that registers SIPs must give you a way to cancel, and fund house and registrar websites must allow it too. Fund houses must cancel within two business days of your request. If a debit had already been set in motion, the money comes back to you.


For card and UPI mandates, you can withdraw the e-mandate or change its validity period whenever you like. Your bank must also let you opt out of a single debit. UPI apps let you view, revoke, pause or change a mandate, and move one to another app once in a rolling 90 days.


Cancelling a SIP ends that SIP and stops its future instalments only. Units already bought are not sold. They stay invested until you redeem them. Restarting means registering a new SIP, and a one-time mandate can be reused for it.


Changing the amount or date varies. Some fund houses modify a SIP in place under a one-time mandate, and others treat a change as a new SIP. A new amount must still fit under the mandate's limit.


Koshex customers can pause, cancel, change the amount of, change the date of, and step up a SIP on Koshex. For the full routes, see[how to stop or pause a SIP](https://koshex.com/blog/how-to-stop-or-pause-a-sip) . Browse funds on[our mutual funds page](https://koshex.com/mutual-funds) .
